questions.prompt: Put the bracketed word in the correct form: "The foreman insisted on the ___ of every worker on the site. (SAFE)"

options.text: safe
safely
safeness
safety

questions.explanation: The gap stands after the and before of, and that slot belongs to a noun; the noun English builds on safe is "safety". "safe" is the adjective itself and cannot follow the. "safely" is the adverb, which describes a verb, not a slot after an article. "safeness" applies a regular ending to a word that already has its own noun, and the rule is to recall the existing word rather than to invent an ending.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Hundreds of pupils reached school late ___ the bus drivers had gone on strike."

options.text: although
because
however
so

questions.explanation: What follows the gap is the cause of what comes before it, and the linker that introduces a cause is "because". "so" points the other way: it must be followed by the result, so it would make the strike the consequence of the late arrivals. "although" opens a clause that contradicts the main one, and a strike does not contradict pupils arriving late. "however" announces a contrast and, in any case, does not join two clauses inside one sentence like this.

questions.prompt: Turn this sentence into the passive: "A local company repairs the school buses."

options.text: The school buses are repairing by a local company.
The school buses is repaired by a local company.
The school buses are repaired by a local company.
The school buses repaired by a local company.

questions.explanation: The passive is be plus the past participle, and the new subject, the school buses, is plural in the present, which gives "The school buses are repaired by a local company." "The school buses are repairing by a local company." keeps an active -ing form and turns the buses into the repairers. "The school buses is repaired by a local company." hands a plural subject a singular be. "The school buses repaired by a local company." has no auxiliary at all, so it is not a sentence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence tells you that the shop is still open today?

options.text: The shop has been open for eleven years.
The shop has been opened eleven years ago.
The shop opened eleven years ago.
The shop was open for eleven years.

questions.explanation: A period that starts in the past and reaches today takes the present perfect, with for before a length of time: "The shop has been open for eleven years." "The shop opened eleven years ago." reports the opening day alone and says nothing about today. "The shop was open for eleven years." shuts the whole period inside the past, so the shop has closed. "The shop has been opened eleven years ago." puts a present perfect beside ago, a moment named in the past, which that tense always refuses.

options.text: More ... better
The more ... the best
The more ... the more better
The more ... the better

questions.explanation: Two changes that move together take the double comparative, the + comparative in each half, and the comparative of well is better: "The more ... the better". "More ... better" drops the two the's that hold the structure up. "The more ... the best" puts a superlative in the second half, which would compare her with a whole group instead of measuring a second change. "The more ... the more better" doubles the comparative: better already carries the idea that more would add.

questions.prompt: The coach said to the parents: "We train here every evening." Which report of his words is correct?

options.text: The coach said the parents that they trained there every evening.
The coach told to the parents that they trained there every evening.
The coach told the parents that they trained there every evening.
The coach told the parents that we trained here every evening.

questions.explanation: Tell is followed straight by the person, with no to, and the report moves we to they and here to there: "The coach told the parents that they trained there every evening." "The coach said the parents that…" uses say with the person right after it, which English never allows: you say something to somebody. "The coach told to the parents that…" adds the to that tell refuses. "The coach told the parents that we trained here every evening." keeps we and here, the words of the man standing on that pitch, so the sentence now claims that the reporter trains there too.
